en.title: Avengers: Doomsday's Latverian Witches: Comic Roots Hinted By Directors
en.summary: Mysterious hooded figures in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday have sparked fan speculation. Directors confirm their origins lie within Marvel comics, promising new depths to their story.
en.body:
The marketing for **Avengers: Doomsday** is dripping with intrigue, and perhaps no element has captured the imagination quite like the shadowy, hooded figures identified as Doctor Doom's Latverian Witches. These enigmatic figures have been a constant presence in trailers and promotional materials, yet their identities and roles remain shrouded in mystery. Fortunately, directors Joe and Anthony Russo have offered a tantalizing clue: their origins are deeply rooted in Marvel comics.

In a recent interview, Joe Russo stated, "His relationship to that dark magic and the witches are an extension of that world [of Latveria]." He further elaborated, "They do have a history that is from the books and [a history] that is a surprise." This revelation is particularly fascinating because, as it stands, there is no established group explicitly named "Latverian Witches" in the Marvel comic archives. This suggests that while the film draws inspiration from existing lore, it will also be weaving in new narrative threads and potentially reinterpreting established characters or concepts to fit the cinematic universe.

## Unpacking the Comic Connections

The absence of a direct comic counterpart doesn't mean the concept is entirely without precedent. Theories are already swirling among the fanbase, connecting these witches to various powerful magic-users within Marvel's vast mythology. One prominent fan theory links them to **Wanda Maximoff**, the Scarlet Witch, given her immense magical power and complex history with characters like Doctor Doom and her own ties to dark magic. Another possibility, though less explored in mainstream discussion, could be a connection to **Cynthia von Doom**, Victor Von Doom's mother, who has been depicted with mystical abilities and a significant influence on her son's magical development. The directors' comments about a "surprise" history hint that the film might be drawing from more obscure corners of the Marvel canon or even creating a composite of different magical elements to build this new coven.

## Fan Speculation and the Multiverse

The mention of Latverian Witches immediately ignites the fan community's passion for deep lore. For seasoned readers, it's an exciting puzzle, a chance to pore over back issues and forgotten storylines to unearth potential origins. For newer fans, it's an invitation to discover the rich tapestry of magic that exists within the Marvel universe, beyond the cosmic and the super-powered. The idea that Doctor Doom, already a formidable intellect and technological genius, also commands dark magic through a mysterious coven adds another layer of menace and complexity to his anticipated role in **Avengers: Doomsday**. This move also aligns with broader trends in superhero storytelling, where the lines between science, magic, and interdimensional power continue to blur, promising a visually spectacular and narratively dense film.

## What's Next

With **Avengers: Doomsday** slated for release, fans will be eagerly awaiting further details or official confirmations regarding the Latverian Witches. The film promises to expand Doctor Doom's character and his sorcerous capabilities, hinting at a significant shift in the cosmic and magical landscape of the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

The hooded figures have been prominently featured in Doomsday ’s marketing (and the most recent Doomsday trailer ), but Marvel has stopped short of telling us who they are or what role they will play. According to Russo, though, the witches’ identities and origins are rooted in Marvel comics, though the film will add some dimensions to their backstories. “His relationship to that dark magic and the witches are an extension of that world [of Latveria],” Russo says. “They do have a history that is from the books and [a history] that is a surprise.” That’s admittedly not much to go on when taken at face value, but that “books” line and a few other things we know about Doomsday may help us make a few educated guesses about what is going on. First off, it’s very much worth noting that there are actually no Latverian Witches in the Marvel comics. That is to say that there is no established group with that name that is associated with Doctor Doom. So what does Joe Russo mean when he says that they have a history from the books? There are a few notable possibilities. First up is the 1989 story Doctor Strange and Doctor Doom: Triumph and Torment , which deals with Doom’s mother being captured by Mephisto, which forces him and Doctor Strange to team up in order to rescue her. This comic was a major turning point in the history of Doom’s relationship with magic. Joe Russo noted in that Entertainment Weekly interview that Doom turns to “a very dark and ancient magic” following a tragic loss in the movie. In the comics, it was the death of Doom’s mother (who was herself a Latverian witch) that inspired much of his pursuit of magic in the first place. Another seemingly relevant possibility as it concerns the witches comes from the 2010 story Avengers: The Children’s Crusade . This is the book that explored a close relationship between Scarlet Witch and Doctor Doom, which is notable for two reasons. The first is the fact that one of VisionQuest ’s post-credits scenes showed Doom seemingly resurrecting Scarlet Witch. The second has something to do with one of the witches’ scarlet robes.
